final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
TO: General Counsel Janet Morales | RE: Proposed termination of Marcus D. Washington, SVP Operations | BASIS: documents supplied (latest dated June 3, 2024)

1. BOTTOM LINE
Do not proceed on the June 10, 2024 timetable, and do not terminate for Cause. The record shows (a) a documented protected-activity sequence (internal safety complaint, OSHA 11(c) complaint, workers' compensation claim), (b) CEO statements that read as age-based, (c) a PIP closed out contrary to the Handbook and to how two younger comparators were treated, and (d) shifting rationales (restructuring vs. performance vs. "explore Cause"). Overall litigation risk of an immediate termination: HIGH. Cause termination: VERY HIGH risk, with little upside. A without-Cause exit under Section 4.2 is contractually clean but does not by itself reduce statutory exposure; the best course is a deliberate, negotiated separation after remedial steps (Part 7). Contract severance owed on any without-Cause exit is roughly $375,000 and should be treated as a sunk cost, not the thing to save.

Caveat: web research was blocked by the proxy, so citations are from knowledge and unverified; cite-check before reliance. The file is dated mid-2024; update limitations periods (e.g., 30 days for OSHA 11(c)) if read later.

2. KEY FACTS
Age 58; hired 2002; SVP since 2016; 19 reviews never below Meets; five Exceeds; Leader of the Year 2015, 2019. Nov 15, 2023: Kessler "we need leaders who grew up with technology." Dec 2023: Washington objects to Lean 2.0 safety changes. Jan 8, 2024: written internal safety complaint. Jan 22: Kessler says Washington "is from a different era... doesn't have the runway left"; HR warned it looks age-related; no retraction. Feb 2: Safety Committee substantially validates complaint; Feb 5: Ostrowski calls it slow-walking. Feb 15: first-ever Needs Improvement, faulting him for "publicly question[ing] the safety implications." Mar 5: OSHA 11(c) complaint (HR copied Mar 6). Mar 18: 60-day PIP. Apr 3: workers' compensation claim (shoulder, no lost time). May 17-20: HR finds 1 of 3 objectives met, 8 of 12 sites done (four blocked by OSHA inspections), cost down 6.4% vs 12%; recommends 30-day extension; Kessler refuses. May 22: HR warns of OSHA, comp, age and process risks. May 28: restructuring memo. June 3: Kessler reaffirms June 10 and asks to "explore... Cause" to avoid "the full severance obligation." No written PIP closure.

3. CONTRACT ANALYSIS (Employment Agreement, June 15, 2016; Illinois law; AAA arbitration, Chicago)
a) Without Cause (Sec. 4.2): requires not less than 30 days' prior written notice, delivered per Sec. 8.5 (courier/certified mail; Executive's address on file). A June 10 date from a June 3 decision cannot comply unless the Company pays in lieu or accepts breach risk. Severance (conditioned on Exhibit A release): 12 months' base ($287,000); pro-rata target bonus (35% = $100,450; about $44,460 if terminated June 10, 162/366 days, "based on actual Company performance," a drafting ambiguity to resolve); 12 months COBRA (estimate $2,340/month in 2016, so at least $28,080, likely more now); outplacement up to $15,000. Estimated total about $374,500 plus Accrued Obligations (confirm whether the FY2023 bonus was paid or reduced after the review).
b) For Cause (Sec. 4.3): none of the five prongs fits. (i)-(iii) felony, willful misconduct causing material harm, fraud: no facts. (iv) material breach: no notice or cure. (v) continued failure to perform: requires written notice and at least 30 days to cure. The PIP is the Company's only argument for notice/cure, but HR's own contemporaneous assessment is "substantial progress," shortfalls were partly outside his control, and the cost target was set without operations input and measured over a 47-day window. Mandatory procedure also is unmet: Board majority vote at a convened meeting, written statement of basis, and 10 business days' notice before the meeting with a right to be heard with counsel. A defective Cause termination is a breach, and the Agreement's own Section 8.8 and the arbitrator's remedial authority (Sec. 7.1) leave the Company paying severance plus fees and facing a pretext narrative. Kessler's June 3 email is damaging and likely discoverable.
c) Position "elimination": the restructuring memo eliminates the title but transfers all 12 facilities to Ostrowski (new title SVP Operations and CI, salary $225,000 to $310,000) and adds a $175,000 director; net leadership cost rises $132,550. That is replacement, not elimination, and it undercuts any economic-RIF defense. The memo also relies on the PIP cost result, conflating performance and restructuring. A non-renewal or without-Cause exit still triggers Sec. 4.2 severance (Sec. 3.1).
d) Irregularities: preamble names Saxonbrook but signature block says Vanguard Logistics Solutions, Inc.; the copy supplied is unsigned; PIP cites Handbook Sec. 7.4 though PIP rules appear at Sec. 5.2. Obtain the executed agreement and full Handbook.
e) Arbitratione) Arbitration (Art. 7) covers statutory claims but does not bind OSHA or EEOC/IDHR (EEOC v. Waffle House, 534 U.S. 279 (2002)).
f) Covenants (Art. 5): the 2016 agreement predates the 2022 Freedom to Work Act amendments (820 ILCS 90), so common-law reasonableness applies (Reliable Fire v. Arredondo, 2011 IL 111871); enforcement against a pretextually terminated executive is difficult. Consider waiver as a bargaining chip.

4. STATUTORY AND COMMON-LAW EXPOSURE
A. OSHA 11(c), 29 U.S.C. 660(c); 29 CFR Part 1977. Protected activity includes internal safety complaints to the employer (29 CFR 1977.9(c)) as well as the agency complaint. No private right of action; the Secretary of Labor sues for reinstatement, back pay and damages. Seventh Circuit courts apply a but-for/"substantial reason" causation test with burden-shifting. Strengths for Washington: knowledge (Kessler received the Jan 8 complaint and Ostrowski's Feb 5 email; HR received OSHA copy Mar 6); first adverse action (Feb 15 review) cites the safety objection as a deficiency, which is near-direct evidence; the Safety Committee validated the concern; the PIP's principal objective was implementing the very Lean 2.0 changes he challenged; PIP and later termination follow within weeks to months; the investigation is open, so termination now is a fresh adverse act and would draw immediate OSHA amendment. Company's defenses: Kessler's displeasure pre-dated the safety complaint (Nov 15 meeting; metric misses; Ostrowski resistance). That defense is double-edged because the pre-complaint motive described is "fresh energy"/"grew up with technology," i.e., age.
B. Illinois Whistleblower Act, 740 ILCS 174. For 2024 events, Sec. 15(c) (retaliation for refusing to participate in activity that would violate a law or regulation) fits his refusal to implement changes he believed would violate OSHA standards; Sec. 15(b) (disclosure to a government agency) fits the OSHA complaint. Remedies: reinstatement, back pay with interest, damages and fees (Sec. 30). The Act was amended effective Jan 1, 2025 to broaden coverage (including internal disclosures); confirm which version governs by date of adverse action.
C. Illinois common-law retaliatory discharge (Palmateer v. International Harvester, 85 Ill. 2d 124 (1981)) for safety whistleblowing, and workers' compensation retaliation, 820 ILCS 305/4(h) and Kelsay v. Motorola, 74 Ill. 2d 172 (1978). Tort remedies include punitive damages, not capped by statute, and the at-will clause in Sec. 3.2 is no defense. Under Clemons v. Mechanical Devices, 184 Ill. 2d 328 (1998), a valid non-pretextual reason defeats causation. The workers' compensation theory is the weakest: the claim was filed after the PIP began, is a gradual-onset claim with no lost time, and the pre-existing plan to remove him predates it. It still adds a compounding timing fact, and HR's description of an "on-site injury" is imprecise.
D. Age: ADEA, 29 U.S.C. 623(a), 631; Illinois Human Rights Act, 775 ILCS 5/2-102. ADEA requires but-for causation (Gross v. FBL Financial, 557 U.S. 167 (2009)); courts assess evidence as a whole (Ortiz v. Werner Enterprises, 834 F.3d 760 (7th Cir. 2016)). Kessler is the decision-maker and her statements are tied to this very decision: "runway left," "different era," "set in his ways," "grew up with technology," "next generation," "energy"; the Board memo repeats that Ostrowski "grew up in a data-driven environment" and offers "runway." "Runway" refers to remaining career, i.e., age proxy, not merely tenure . Plaintiff is 58 and replaced by a younger person (Ostrowski's age to be confirmed; O'Connor v. Consolidated Coin Caterers, 517 U.S. 308 (1996)). HR warned Kessler in writing-adjacent notes and she did not retract: willfulness risk, supporting ADEA liquidated (double) damages under 29 U.S.C. 626(b). Charge deadlines: 300 days (EEOC/IDHR).
E. Pretext evidence: shifting reasons (performance, restructuring, Cause); first poor rating after 19 good ones under a new CEO; skipped progressive-discipline steps; PIP unclosed though Handbook 5.2.3 bars action until written closure; younger comparators Kolb (34) and Okafor (41) received extensions and written closure. The Company may say they were in other departments, but deviation from a department-neutral policy is pretext evidence; PIP target set without operations input and sites blocked by OSHA inspections.
F. Company defenses: genuine reorganization within business judgment; documented missed targets; full PIP; Board involvement; Kolb was also terminated. Credible only if reasons are consistent and procedure regularized.

5. PRIVILEGE AND EVIDENCE
HR notes, the email chain (counsel copied only from May 22), safety records and PIP are ordinary business records; the "work product" legend on the OSHA compilation does not shield them from OSHA, the EEOC or an arbitrator. Only legal-advice communications are protected. Ms. Morales is a potential fact witness; consider outside counsel for the investigation. Ms. Chandrasekaran is a favorable witness for Washington and engaged in protected opposition; take no adverse action against her. A litigation hold is overdue (OSHA investigation open since March): Kessler, Ostrowski, Chandrasekaran, Morales, Hensley, Board materials, texts, handwritten Nov 15 notes.

6. RISK RATING (judgment)
Contract (no Cause, notice cured): low; Cause asserted: very high. OSHA 11(c)/Illinois whistleblower: high (direct language in review). Age: high. Workers' compensation retaliation: low to moderate. Adverse-outcome range: severance (~$375,000) plus 2-3 years back/front pay on $387,450 (about $0.8-1.2 million), ADEA liquidated doubling, uncapped tort punitives and fees; plausibly $1.5-3 million plus defense costs.

7. RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Stop the June 10 date; take no step toward Cause. Remove the "explore Cause to avoid severance" objective in writing from the work stream.
2. Issue a litigation hold immediately; direct Kessler and Ostrowski to stop creating non-privileged commentary about Washington.
3. Brief the full Board (or independent directors) on facts omitted from the May 28 memo: OSHA complaint, Safety Committee findings, workers' compensation claim, HR's warnings, age remarks, comparator data. Board approval on an incomplete record increases risk and governance exposure.
4. Interview-based independent review (outside counsel, not Kessler/Ostrowski) of the retaliation and age allegations.
5. Choose the path:
 Option A (lowest legal risk, may be commercially unwelcome): extend the PIP 30 days as HR recommended, adjust Objective 1 for the OSHA-blocked sites, close it in writing under Sec. 5.2.3, adopt the Safety Committee's recommendations on Changes 1 and 3, and reassess on a clean record.
 Option B (recommended if the Company is committed to separation): negotiated without-Cause exit under Sec. 4.2 with full written notice, enhanced consideration (for example, additional months of pay, waiver or narrowing of non-compete), mutual non-disparagement, and a comprehensive release. The release must satisfy the OWBPA (29 U.S.C. 626(f): 21 days, 7-day revocation, advice to consult counsel; Exhibit A already does this), carve out agency charges, and, because an 11(c) complaint is pending, be paired with an OSHA-approved settlement or withdrawal; any confidentiality term must comply with the Illinois Workplace Transparency Act (820 ILCS 96). Do not condition Accrued Obligations on the release.
 Option C (not recommended): unilateral without-Cause termination with 30-day notice and severance, no negotiation. Contract-compliant but leaves all statutory claims open and creates a new adverse act during the OSHA investigation.
6. Align the narrative: choose one true rationale. If the role is truly being restructured, do not simultaneously assert performance failure; do not present as "elimination" if the duties pass to Ostrowski. Correct age-coded language in all further documents; train Kessler.
7. Confirm the executed Agreement, corporate entity, full Handbook and PIP check-in records.

8. OPEN ITEMS
Ostrowski's age; Kessler's knowledge dates; Board minutes; PIP check-in records; OSHA investigation status; FY2023 bonus status.
